items: The Shrine of Neby Yûnas, at El Meshhad.  This is one of the many Moslem sanctuaries in Syria dedicated to the Prophet Jonah
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Jonah (Biblical prophet)
The Horns of Hattîn (Kûrûn Hattîn).  The summit of the eastern horn is a little circular plain; and the top of the lower ridge between the two horns is also level
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Northern end of the Sea of Galilee, from the Castle of Tiberias.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Mosque of Tiberias (Tûbarîyeh).  This is a good example of the appearance of "grass on house-tops."
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Castle of Tiberias (Tûbarîyeh), showing the damage done by the earthquake of 1837
Hot baths of Tiberias (Hûmmâm Tûbarîyeh), with the town of Tiberias and Khân Minyeh in the distance. The interior of the public bath is shown, with its pierced dome and marble pavement.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Filmer, John
The Valley of Pigeons (Wâdy el Hamâm).  The bed of this picturesque valley runs towards the Lake of Tiberias just north of Mejdel
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Kûl'at ibn Ma'ân, on the north-west side of the Valley of Pigeons. This castle consists of caverns connected by passages; opposite to it stands Irbid, the ancient Arbela
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Palmer, William James; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Magdala (Mejdel).  Beyond the village is the fertile plain of Gennesaret. It is three miles long and one mile in width.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Fishermen on the Sea of Galilee.  The lake contains many good kinds of fish, some of which, it is said, do not occur elsewhere except in tropical climates
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Plain of Gennesaret, from Khân Minyeh.  The town of Tiberias in the distance, and Mejdel (Magdala) on the right, at the southern extremity of the plain
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The Sea of Galilee from 'Ain et Tîn, the fountain of the fig-tree, near Khân Minyeh, the supposed site of Capernaum.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
On the shore of the lake, at Et Tâbighah, the supposed site of Bethsaida, an oleander in full bloom grows among the rocks, and storks are characteristically hovering over the lake
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The Sea of Galilee from Et Tâbighah, the supposed site of Bethsaida.  The dilapidated mill in the foreground is one of several which were built here by the celebrated Sheikh Dhaher el 'Amr, to utilise the copious streams for which this place is famous
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Johnstone, J.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
View from Tell Hûm, with fishing-boat.  There is no sign of any harbour having been constructed here, and in stormy weather it would be difficult to effect a landing at this spot
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)

The ruins of Tell Hûm.  By several authorities the place is regarded as the site of Capernaum. The principle building, of which remains exist, was constructed of white limestone, but the ruins around it are of black basalt.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Caverns in the cliffs of Wâdy Leimôn.  The upper portion of Wâdy el Amûd, the Valley of the Column
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The cliffs of Wâdy Leimôn, pierced with holes in which a great variety of birds find safe retreat. The bed of the valley is in some places very narrow and difficult to traverse.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Lauderbach, James W.; Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Safed, one of the four holy places of the Jews in Palestine; showing the Jewish quarter on the western and north-western side of the hill, just below the castle
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Johnston, J. (fl. 188-); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Castle of Safed, on the northern crest of the hill, with the Moslem quarter in the foreground
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Whymper
Ancient synagogue, Meirôn, situated on the top of an overhanging cliff, which was levelled artificially. Only the south front is now standing.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Badoureau, Ed.

Jewish shrine at Meirôn.  The town of Safed appears on the hill beyond, and on the right there is a glimpse of the Sea of Galilee. During the annual festival pilgrims burn shawls, robes, and kerchiefs, more or less costly, at this venerated shrine.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Remains of a synagogue at Kefr Beirim.  The village of Beirim, with its remarkable ruins, stands on the summit of a peak north-west of Meirôn. Its present inhabitants are chiefly Maronites
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Site of Kedesh Naphtali.  Marked by remains of buildings of Jewish and Roman origin, and by a small village called Kedes. The spring used by the villagers is shown in the foreground. Mount Hermon is seen in the distance.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Lachs?; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Tomb at Kedes, the ancient Kedesh Naphtali.  Thirty-five feet square; piers at the corners support round arches twenty-one feet high. Between the arches were the places for internment, three between each and one on either side of the door. The arches were formerly walled up and the building was covered with a dome.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Sarcophagi among the ruins of Kedesh Naphtali.  The one in the foreground is a good example of a sarcophagus with two receptacles.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
First glimpse of the Lebanon range from the south, with the ruined fortress of Hunîn and its clusters of one-storied houses in the foreground
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Lake Hûleh (Waters of Merom) from Hunîn, looking towards the south-east, with the uneven table-land of Jaulân (Gaulanitis) in the distance
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The River Hasbâny, the northern tributary of the Jordan, fringed with oleanders and willows, and crossed by the Jisr el Ghûjar
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The site of Laish, afterwards called Dan, the ancient northern limit of the Holy Land, at the most westernly source of the Jordan. This spot is now known as Tell el Kâdy (the Hill of the Judge), and here stands a sacred oak hung with votive offerings, with a tomb dedicated to Sheikh Merzûk.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Johnston, J. (fl. 188-)
The Jordan at Bâniâs (Cæsarea Philippi).  Bâniâs is merely the Arabic pronunciation of the ancient Panias of the Greeks and Romans. In the foreground is a peasant carrying a plough.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Remains of a Roman aqueduct at Bâniâs (Cæsarea Philippi), overgrown with thistles and reeds, and crowned with an evergreen oak
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Badoureau, Ed.

The most easterly source of the Jordan, Bâniâs (Cæsarea Philippi).  This place has justly been called a Syrian Tivoli. The cliff is of ruddy limestone mingled with basalt. On a platform of the rock stands the wely of Sheikh Khidr (Saint George)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Sculptured niches dedicated to Pan, at Cæsarea Philippi, in the face of the cliff, south of the cavern from which the Jordan springs. A peasant with his double-reed Pandean pipes and his flock of long-eared sheep appropriately occupies the foreground.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Harley

Bowers on the housetops at Bâniâs (Cæsarea Philippi).  The present village consists of fifty or sixty houses. In summer-time the inhabitants sleep in their bowers, nearly every house being provided with one or two.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Annin, Phineas F.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Bertrand, C. (fl. 188-)
The Castle of Subeibeh, known also as the Castle of Bâniâs
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The citadel of the Castle of Subeibeh, from within the castle walls, which enclose an olive-grove. It is two thousand three hundred feet above the sea-level.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

A cup of coffee on the heights of Subeibeh.  All the implements for preparing it are shown in the foreground - the iron saucer in which to roast the berries, the pestle and mortar for pounding them, and the water boiling on the fire of crackling twigs
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Moslem graves under 'The Oaks of Bashan.'  At Tell Hazûr, near Bâniâs. There appears to have been a complete circle of evergreen oaks here, surrounding a temple or an altar. It is still regarded as a holy "place," and is now dedicated to Sheikh Othmân of Hazûr. A group of ruins called Hazûr exists not far from this spot.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harper, Henry A. (Henry Andrew) (1836-1900); Bradshaw, Samuel, engraver
The Nahr Leddân, an affluent of the Jordan.  It joins the stream from Bâniâs four miles south of Tell el Kâdy
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Palmer, William James

Pottery, Râsheiyet el Fûkhâr; this place, as its name implies, is famous for its potter's clay. Its furnaces are dome-shaped and capable of burning enormous jars. The potter, mounted on a high seat, sets the wheel in motion with his foot and shapes the clay with his hand. The man beyond is adding handles to the jars.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The ruins of the temple at Hebbâriyeh.  Showing the eastern portal, which faced Mount Hermon, exactly opposite the valley of Shib'a
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Lauderbach, James W.
Wâdy Shib'a, from Hebbâriyeh.  The village of Shib'a may be seen on the summit of the second peak; it is the highest inhabited place in Mount Hermon (Jebel esh Sheikh)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The gateway, Hâsbeiya.  The town is two thousand two hundred feet above the sea-level, on the west side of an amphitheatre of hills covered to their summits with vineyards, orchards, and olive groves
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Palace of Hâsbeiya.  Scene of a terrible massacre of Christians on June 3rd, 1860. The fountain if Hâsbeiya forms a copious stream which flows into the Hâsbany.
El Kûweh, the natural bridge over the Lîtâny.  It is formed of a number of fallen rocks, which have left a passage of about one hundred feet in height for the stream below
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Measom, A.

The gorge of the Lîtâny.  The precipices are in some places nearly one thousand feet in height. The banks are overgrown with sycamores, myrtles, and various shrubs, and eagles build their nests in the inaccessible cliffs.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Mount Hermon from Râsheiya.  The name Hermon (like harem) signifies "unapproachable," or "the holy." The Sidonians called this Mount Sirion. The Arabic name Jebel esh Sheikh means "mountain of the aged" or "of the white-headed." It is also called Jebel eth Thelj, the "snow mountain."
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The Castle of Râsheiya.  The scene of a terrible massacre of Christians on June 4th, 1860

Medallion on the temple at Rûkhleh, outside the south wall, near the east corner; it is five feet in diameter. The upper part has been destroyed by gunpowder. The neighbouring village is inhabited by Druses
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The temple at Deir el 'Ashâir.  It stands on a platform of massive masonry, one hundred and twenty-six feet long by sixty-nine feet wide, and about twenty feet high on the eastern side, which faces Mount Hermon. The village is inhabited by a few families of Druses and Christians.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The gorge of the Bûrada (Abana), through which the new French road approaches Damascus.  At the outlet of this gorge the stream is divided into seven branches, two of which supply the fountain in the city, and the rest are used to irrigate the fields and gardens.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Orr, Nathaniel

Entrance to Damascus, by the road through the Merj, or meadow, west of the city. The large building on the right, with its many domes and two slender minarets, is the Tekîyeh, or hospital for pilgrims, built by Sultan Selim I in A.D. 1516.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Werner, Karl Friedrich Heinrich, 1808-1894 (1808-1894); Saddler, John (1813-1892)

Roadside café, Damascus.  The man in the foreground is selling thin loaves of wheaten bread, slightly spread with butter and grape syrup and sprinkled with sessame seed. He calls out every now and then, in a plaintive voice, "God is the nourisher! Buy my bread!"
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

A Mueddin chanting the call to prayer from a gallery of the Minaret of 'Isa (Jesus).  This minaret (on the summit of which Moslem tradition says that Jesus will appear on the Judgement Day) is at the south-east corner of the Great Mosque, Damascus, and is two hundred and fifty feet in height. The beautiful octagonal minaret at the south-west corner is called El Gharbîyeh. A third minaret, not shown in this illustration, is called El 'Arûs (the Bride).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Kubbet el Khazneh (Dome of the Treasures), Damascus.  In the west part of the court of the Great Mosque. It is said to contain ancient books and other relics which are held sacred.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Johnstone, J.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The tomb of Saladin, Damascus.  This mausoleum, which is just outside the north-west corner of the Great Mosque, is jealously guarded, and it is difficult to gain access to it. The south-western minaret of the Great Mosque can be seen through the archway.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Mosque of Sabunîyeh, Damascus, built of course of black basalt and white limestone
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Gold and Silver Smiths' Bazaar, Damascus.  A large nearly square court; the blackened roof is supported by arches and massive piers. It is so noisy that sales are often effected by means of signs. The man in the foreground holds up three fingers to show that he will sell a certain article for three pieces of money, the buyer (a veiled woman) offers two.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The Mohammedan day school in the Shoemakers' Bazaar.  The pupils are seated on the floor of a shop, each holding a wooden tablet, on which the lesson is written; and they intone it together, rocking themselves to and fro all the while
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Arch of Triumph, Damascus.  At the western side of the Great Mosque, as seen from a roof of a house in the Book Bazaar. When entire its width was eighty feet and its height seventy feet.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Bridge in the Shoemakers' Bazaar, Damascus.  A camel and a little group of people can be seen through the grated window, passing over the bridge. In the foreground there is a pleasantly situated café.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
A narrow by-way in Damascus.  The upper stories and projecting windows are constructed of poplar stems, filled in with sun-dried bricks, placed diagonally and plastered over with clay
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Orr, Nathaniel

The citadel, Damascus.  A large oblong structure surrounded by a moat. There are twelve projecting towers, two of which are shown above. In the foreground there is a café, in the upper balcony of which a turbaned player holds up a winning card exultingly.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley

Mosque of the Tekîyeh, or Hospice of the Sultan Selim.  Its position is shown in the illustration on page 381. The court is planted with walnut-trees. The cloisters and interior of the mosque are decorated with exceedingly fine glazed tiles.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)
Makbaret Bâb es Saghîr (Burial-Ground of the Little Gate).  Tradition says that two of the wives of Mohammed were interned here. A modern domed structure marks the spot.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The Horse Bazaar, Damascus, as it appears on market days.  In the foreground is a Bedouin sheikh on horseback, fully equipped. Another Bedouin has just dismounted to greet a friend, exemplifying the words, "and he fell upon his neck and kissed him."

The large plane-tree, Damascus.  It is nearly forty feet in circumference. A peasant and his plough are resting against it, and in its shade a carperter is working, steadying his bow saw with his naked foot.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Werner, Karl Friedrich Heinrich, 1808-1894 (1808-1894); Bertrand, C. (fl. 188-)

Houses on the city wall, Damascus.  On the south-east side, belonging to the Jewish quarter. The Bâb Kisân, which is not far from this spot, is now a disused and closed-up gate. It stands on the site of a much more ancient one.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Bâb Shurky (East Gate), Damascus, an ancient Roman portal with three arches. The central and southern ones are now built up; the northern arch, now in use, is concealed by the Saracenic Gate, at right-angles with it. The Great Mosque can be seen in the distance.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Jâmi` al-Umawî al-Kabîr (Damascus, Syria)
'The street called Straight," it runs westward from the East Gate, dividing the Christian from the Jewish quarter. The Mohammedans call it "Sultan's Highway."
Bâb Tûma, the Gate of Thomas.  An inscription states that it was erected in A.H. 634 (A.D. 1237). It leads out of the city towards the north-east road, the caravan route to Aleppo and Palmyra.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
A street barber's stall, with a ragged canopy ready for use as protection from sun or rain. The street barber is only employed by those who are too poor to go to the commodious barbers' shops.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Closson, William Baxter Palmer (1848-1926); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Bedouins buying spears in the Sûk es Sinânîyeh, which is the great emporium for all the requirements of Bedouins and peasants, including all kinds of primitive weapons and clothing
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Reception room of a Damascus house, showing the lower portion of it only, with its fountain and marble pavement. The upper part of the room, where guests are received, is eighteen inches higher, and is furnished with cushions and carpets. An incense burner is standing at the extreme edge of the daïs.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Whymper

A street drinking-fountain, Damascus.  The lady who is riding en cavalier wears a dark muslin veil, called a mandîl, which quite conceals her features; her outer garment, an izzar, is like a large sheet of fine white calico, and in this she envelopes herself completely.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Greek inscription on an ancient and disused doorway of the Great Mosque.  In the south wall; it can only be seen from the roof of the Silversmiths' Bazaar. The words are, "Thy kingdom, O Christ, is an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion endureth throughout all generations."
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Jâmi` al-Umawî al-Kabîr (Damascus, Syria)

A Bedouin of the Haurân. Bedouins (more correctly Bedawîn) occupy the north-west district of the Haurân; the plain is inhabited by peasants, and the Druses for many centuries have colonised the mountain range
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)

Ruined tombs, Palmyra, in the Wâdy el Kûbûr. The largest one, on the right, is eighty feet high. There is an inscription on it which states that it was built as a family tomb by Elabelos, in the Seleucian year 414 (A.D. 102).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Johnstone, J.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Grand Colonnade, Palmyra, from the triumphal arch.  Showing the syenite columns of the Tetrapylon; the prostate one is thirty feet long and three feet in diameter. In the distance the ancient city wall, known as the Wall of Justinian, can be traced.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Palmer, William James

Western side of the ruins of the Temple of the Sun, Palmyra, showing part of the double colonnade which formed the cloisters of the temple. The brackets projecting from the columns, about two-thirds of the way up, formerly supported statues.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Ruins of a mausoleum near the north-western end of the Great Colonnade, Palmyra.  In the interior there is a large sarcophagus richly ornamented with sculptured satyrs and garlands of flowers and fruit; another mausoleum near it, in better preservation, is shown on page 435.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); French, W.

The triumphal arch, Palmyra.  It is about three hundred yards from the north-western corner of the Temple of the Sun, and formed the triple entrance to the Great Colonnade, which appears to have consisted of a broad central avenue with narrow ways on each side.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
View of Palmyra, from the Grand Colonnade, showing the castle in the distance.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Wâdy Barada, from Bessîma.  The village is situated in a little basin formed by a bend of the river, and is entirely shut in by high ledges of rock. The soil is everywhere carefully cultivated. In the foreground the villagers are winnowing grain.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

'Ain Fîjeh. this fountain issues from a cavern with two openings, over one of which there is an arch. It forms at once a rapid stream thirty feet wide and three of four feet deep, which rushes over a rocky bed for eighty yards and then joins the Barada.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wayside tombs in Wâdy Barada.  Where walnut and fig trees yield abundantly, and the oleander flourishes. Rows of poplar trees peering out of the gorge mark its course.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Gathering figs on the Barada, near 'Ain Fîjeh.  Here the effects of irrigation are strikingly seen; as far as the canals and ducts are carried all is luxuriant, but immediately above the line all is parched and bare
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Tombs and aqueduct, Wâdy Barada.  Here the gorge intersects the central ridge of Anti-Lebanon; but as it makes a sharp turn, we only see a deep recess in the mountain-side dotted with tombs
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The cliffs of Sûk Wâdy, Barada.  A modern bridge of a single arch spans the river, and the road crosses from the right to the left bank. This is the narrowest part of the gorge, and the cliffs that shut it in are not more than a hundred feet apart.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)
Road and tablets cut in the cliff of Wâdy Barada.  On the north or left bank of the river
Waterfall of the Upper Barada, near Zebedâny.  Here the stream is augmented by the outfall of Wâdy el Kûrn
The tomb of Noah, at a place called Kerak Nûh. The so-called tomb is probably a portion of an ancient aqueduct.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

An Arab shrine, south-west of Ba'albek.  Called Kubbet Dûris, after the neighbouring village of Dûris; it is a modern structure formed of eight ancient granite columns clumsily set up and surmounted by a heavy architrave. An enormous sarcophagus, standing on end, serves as the mihrab, or Muslim prayer niche.

Entrance to the ruins of Ba'albek.  At the south-west corner, through a long vaulted passage like a railway tunnel under the great platform. Two of these great vaults run parallel with each other, from east to west, and are connected by a third running at right angles to them from north and south.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The Temple of the Sun, Ba'albek.  Showing the north and west sides. The columns, including the capitals, are forty-six and a-half feet in height; they are ten feet from the walls, and support an entablature connected with the cella by large slabs of stone
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Saddler, John (1813-1892)
Under the peristyle, Temple of the Sun, Ba'albek, on the west side, looking towards Lebanon.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The fallen column, Ba'albek.  In the peristyle on the south side of the Temple of the Sun, where only four connected columns remain in situ. Several shafts have fallen from the temple platform into the little orchard below.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Badoureau, Ed.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

South wing of the portico of the Great Temple, Ba'albek.  The floor of the portico is twenty feet above the level of the adjoining ground, and it is probable that it was approached from the east by a broad flight of steps
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Johnstone, J.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Gateway to the Temple of the Sun, Ba'albek.  It is twenty-one feet in width, and forty-two feet high. The modern masonry, which supports the displaced keystone, conceals the crested eagle carved upon its soffit.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Ruined mosque, north of Ba'albek.  Rudely built of ancient materials. There are ten columns of polished red granite and eighteen limestone columns, all surmounted by richly carved limestone capitals.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Badoureau, Ed.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The six columns of the Great Temple, Ba'albek. The winter winds have almost destroyed the carving on the north side of the capitals; but the south side of the capitals and of the entablature, shown above, are in a good state of preservation
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The south-east corner of the Temple of the Sun, Ba'albek.  At the east end of this temple there was a vestibule with a row of fluted columns within the outer line of plain columns; only two of these are now standing
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The Temple of Venus, or circular temple in the village of Ba albek, not far from the south-east corner of the Acropolis. It is now converted into a Muslim shrine, and dedicated to El Barbara.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The large stone in the quarry, Ba'albek called the Hajr el Hûbla. It is sixty-eight feet four inches in length. On the under side it is cut away all round, remaining attached to the bed of the rock in the middle along its entire length.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

A Cedar of Lebanon.  In the distance there is a glimpse of the Mediterranean Sea. The grove consists of about three hundred and fifty trees, the tallest of which are not more than seventy-eight feet in height. In the midst of the grove there is a Maronite chapel.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

In the grove of cedars, Lebanon. The group of cedars occupies the top of a hill with five culminating points of various sizes. The rock on which the trees grow is white limestone, and the decaying spines, cones, and other matter have formed a dark-coloured soil. In the background rise the snow-covered peaks of Dahr el Kodîb; the highest point is ten thousand and fifty feet above the sea-level.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Johnstone, J.
The sea of Galilee, from the heights of Safed
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harper, Henry A. (Henry Andrew) (1836-1900); D. Appleton and Company
Picturesque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt vol. II.  The convent of St. Catherine, Mount Sinai
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Saint Catherine (Monastery : Mount Sinai)
Picturesque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt . . . Volume II [Half title]
Hasrûn, a Maronite village of North Lebanon, on the summit of a precipice on the south side of the gorge of the Kashîda (the sacred river).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The valley of the Kadîsha (the holy river), with  distant view of the Mediterranean Sea and El Mîna (Minet Tarâbalus), the port of Tripoli
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Convent of the Mullawîyeh, or dancing dervishes, Tripoli, with a distant view of the snow crowned summits of Lebanon. In the foreground flows the Kadîsha (the sacred river), called also Nahr Abû Ali. On the pathway may be seen a water-wheel and two millst
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The castle of Tripoli, a stronghold of the crusaders. It was converted into an imperial penitentiary by Midhat Pasha when he was governor-general of Syria. It stands on a narrow ridge, which slopes on the west towards the town, and on the east to the bed of the Kadîsha.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The castle of the Museilihah ("The palace of weapons"). It stands on a precipitous rock by the Nahr el Jozeh, in the middle of a wooded valley, and commands the pass. It was until recently occupied by a band of brigands, the terror of travellers.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Miller, W. (fl. ca. 1880)
The natural bridge of Akura. On front of a cavern from which issues a strem called the Neb'a Ruweis. a triburary of the Adonis (Nahr Ibrahim).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Cliffs of Akura, in the Mogherîye valley, Lebanon. Every available space in the valley is cultivated. On the ledges of the cliffs fruit-trees flourish and wheat is grown.
The fountain of Akfa (Apheca). Source of the Adonis riverr (Nafr Ibrahim). Close to this spot are the remains of a famous temple of Venus, which was destroyed by the order of Constantine.
The gorge of the Kadîsha -- Lebanon
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Bradshaw, Samuel, engraver; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The valley of the Adonis (Nahr Ibrahim). The scenery in this valley was not surpassed by any in Lebanon.  The hillsides are in many places clothed with pines and oak-trees, and groves of mulberry and fruit-trees border the stream.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Lebanon coast near the mouth of the Adonis river. The iron-stained soil of the sandstone strata is annually washed down into the river by the heavy winter rains, and the discolored stream can be traced far out into the blue sea. This gave rise to the belief that the river was tinged with the blood of Adonis, every year in memory of his death.

The natural bridge, Lebanon. It is called in Arabic "Jisr el Hajr" (The Bridge of Stone). It spans the chasm through which flows the Neb'a el Lebban (Fountain of Milk), one of the sources of the Nahr el Kelb (the Dog River).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Palmer, William James
Under the natural bridge, Lebanon. The stream, after passing under the bridge, descends the mountain-side through a glen like a huge fissure, and then dashes over a ledge of rock in sheets of foam.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The chasm of Neb'a el Lebban. Just above the Natural Bridge (Jisr el Hajr).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Palmer, William James; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Roman bridge near Juneh. It spans a little stream called Ma'amiltein, which in the water flows from the hills to the beautiful bay of Juneh. Adjoining the bridge there is a Syrian khan.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Limestone rocks, Ajeltûn, Lebanon. In this district, well named Kesrawan (Broken Region) is a chaos of rugged  mountains, which in some places assume grotesque and in others grand architectural forms. The belfry of the great Convent of Ajeltûn is shown in the background.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Beirût, from Jaita. A beautifully situated village north of the Dog River (Nahr el Kelb), on the heights above the gorge.  In the distance, beyond St. George's Bay, the sandy promontory of Beirût appears.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

A Lebanon café. Pleasantly situated by a mountain stream and sheltered by the dense foliage of the carouba trees (Ceratonia siliqua). The presence of one of these wayside resting places always indicates a good site for an encampment, for it is sure to be near a supply of good water.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Harley
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Cliffs and sculptured tablets. On the rocky promontory whoch projects far into the sea, south of Nahr el Kelb (Dog River), rising to the height of about one hundred feet.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Cousen, Charles (1819-1889)
The Nahr el Kelb (Dog River), and ancient bridge connected with the rock-cut coast. In the summer, the river is fordable here.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Modern aqueduct on the Nahr el Kelb near to which are the newly discovered Assyrian tablets relating to Nebuchadnezzar.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Pigeon rocks, Beirût. In the cliff from which these island rocks have broken away, there is an enormous cavern which can be entered by small boats.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Beirût castle.  Built by the Crusaders, but partly with materials which had been used for earlier structures, for there are many granite columns introduced transversely into the lower part of the walls.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Willmore, Arthur (1814-1888); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Khan Neby Yûnas (The khan of the prophet Jonah). Adjoining a Muslim shrine sacred to his memory. Close to it there is a group of mulberry- trees, and beyond are groves of olives and fig trees belonging to the village of Neby Yûnas, also called El Jûjeh.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Jonah (Biblical prophet)

The castle and the harbour of Saida, the ancient Sidon. Called Kul'at el Bahr (Castle on the Sea). It stands on a rocky island opposite the north-east end of the town, with which it is connected by an embankment with arches.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
The citdel of Saida, the ancient Sidon. Now called Kul'at el Mezzeh. It stands on the south-eastern extremity of the town, on a heap of rubbish in which layers of the purple shell are still visible.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

A peasant woman churning. The churn is made of the tanned skin of a goat stripped off whole; it is partly filled with milk and the extremities being securely closed, it is suspended in any convenient place, by four ropes fastened to the skin of the legs.

Site of Sarepta. As early as the thirteenth century, this city was in ruins, and now only fragments of its foundations exist, chiefly on a headland called 'Ain el Kantarah and also along the shore south of it extending a mile or more. Early Greek and Roman writers speak highly in praise of the [site] of Sarepta
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The Bay of Sideon from Sarepta. The distance from Sarepta to Sidon, in a straight line across the bay, is about ten miles.  On the extreme right, partially covered by a tree, the ruins on Tell el Burâk can be distinguished, and the Khan el Burâk . . .
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Ridge over the Nahr el Kâsimîyeh (the Leontes). On the ancient Roman coast road, which is now traversed by telegraph wires.  Higher up, this river is called El Litâny.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The valley of the Leontes, near the coast. The river, the Nahr el Kâsîmiyeh, is of considerable depth at this point, and flows hence to the sea in a very serpentine course.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Bradshaw, Samuel, engraver
The gate of Tyre (Sûr). There are two springs of fresh water on the peninsula, one of which is close to this gate. It has been conjectured that they are connected with the foundations of Râs el 'Ain.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Ruins of the cathedral church at Tyre. Eusebius describes this building as the most splendid of all the temples of Phoenicia. Among the ruins there is a double column of red  syenite granite, now prostrate, consisting of two parallel connected shafts of great size.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Kabr Hirâm. And the neighboring village of Hanâwieh, with a view of the peninsula of Tyre as it appears from this spot.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Hiram, King of Tyre, fl. 969-936 B.C.

The remains of Tyre. The shore is strewn from one end to the other, along the edge of the water, and in the water, with columns of red and grey granite of various dimensions, the only remaining monuments of ancient Tyre.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Reservoirs of Râs el 'Ain and part of the Roman aqueduct. Close to this spot stood Palaeotyrus of which no vestige now remains, the materials have been carried away by Alexander (332 B.C.) to construct the more or causeway which unites insular Tyre to the mainland.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Aqueduct, Râs el 'Ain. Of Saracenic origin, its slightly pointed arches are in many places almost concealed by luxuriant vegetation.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Râs el Abyad (White Cape), the ladder of Tyre. From the south side. The rock-cut undulating road. with its shallow steps, is in many places nearly two hundred feet above the sea.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Râs el Abyad. Showing the north or Tyrian side. The little tower in the distance is a Turkish guard-house, where tolls are levied, as it commands the pass to Acre.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Looking towards Tyre from Nâkûrah.  An old olive-tree in the foreground and a Muslim cemetary on the hillside.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Râs en Nâkûrah. The road over this headland, which has also been called the "Ladder of Tyre" has lately been greatly improved.  South of it there is a spring called 'Ain Musheirifeh.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The city of Acre (Akka) from the north.  Mount Carmel is seen in the distance, beyond the bay. Muslim cemetary and aqueduct in the foreground.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The city of Acre from the south.  The mount of the Nahr Na'mân, the ancient river Belus, in the foreground, where, tradition says, glass was first produced by an accidental combination of the necessary materials.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Gate of 'Akka (St. Jean d'Acre). It is the only entrance to the city and is situated near the south end of the eastern land wall, close to the head of the shallow harbor.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Ruins of an aqueduct east of Akka. The position of the stork is quite characteristic, as storks instinctively take possession of lofty deserted structures, where they may build their huge nests in safety.

General view of 'Akka from the North- East, Carmel in the distance.  More than half the space within the walls is occupied by government buildings and barracks.  On the right is the great mosque of Jezzar Pasha, with its curiously butressed dome. It stands in a square court surrounded by domed chambers for the use of the mosque attendents and pilgrims. A steamer is approaching the town of Haifa, at the foot of Mount Carmel.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Ablutions after a mid-day meal. Of all the people of the East it may be said, "except they wash their hands diligently, eat not," and after a meal it is urgently necessary when fingers have been used instead of forks.
The plain of 'Akka from the slopes of Carmel. Showing the grove of palm-trees which extends from Haifa nearly as far as the river Kishon.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
A well in a garden of Haifa, Showing a machine, called a sâkiyeh, raising water to fill the adjacent tank, on the right.

The Bay of 'Akka from the slopes of Carmel. With the ruined castle of Haifa in the foreground and a glimpse of the town of Haifa at the foot of the castle-hill ; in the distance the city of 'Akka is clearly shown.

The convent of Mount Carmel.  Its terraced roof commands extensive views alonf the coast, north and south.  The building on the left is used for the accomodation of native pilgrims, and is surmounted by a light house four hundred and seventy feet above the sea.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The grotto known as the "school of the prophets,"  to which pilgrimmages are made by Mohammadans, in honor of Elijah. The house on the left is modern but occupies the site of an ancient chapel.  It is opposite the entrance of the cave.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The northern point of Mount Carmel. With the lighthouse on its summit.  The sandy point is Râs Kerûm (the head of the vineyard).  The city of 'Akka appears in the distance, and beyond it are the white cliffs of  Râs en Nakûrah.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Swain, Joseph Blomeley (b. 1844); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

El Mahrakah, the place of Elijah's sacrifice.  At the south-eastern point of the range of Carmel.  In the foreground is the green knoll called Tell el Kassîs (the Hill of the Priests), close to which the Kishon flows.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Elijah (Biblical prophet)
Well at the place of Elijah's sacrifice, and a view from the heights above it.  Embracing a long line of the coast of the plain of 'Athlit, with a strip of blue sea beyond.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The river Kishon from El Mahrakah. The place of Elijah's sacrifice. A Bedawîn encampment in the foreground, and the hills of Galilee in the distance beyond a forest of oak-trees.
Haifa, at the foot of Mount Carmel.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Brandard, Edward Paxman (1819-1898); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The plains of Esdraelon from the heights above El Mahrakah, looking towards the south-east.  In the distance, in a central position, the village of Zerîn (Jezreel), with its white castle, is easily distinguished.  On the left rises Jebel Duby (Little Hermon), and on the right are the mountains of Gilboa.

The river Kishon. As it appears after the rainy season, where it flows through the narrow pass called Wâdy el Kasab (Valley of Reeds), which leads from the great plain of Esdraelon to the plain of' 'Akka. Oleanders flourish here, and many small birds build their nests.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Athlît, from the south.  Called Castellum Peregrinorum by medieval writers. It was one of the most important landing-places for pigrims during the thirteenth century. It stands on a rocky promontory  which projects a quarter of a mile westward into the sea
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)

Ruins on the west side of Athlît.  The fortress was built by the Templars in the year 1218 and was the last place held by the crusaders in Palestine.  It was taken by the Sultan Melek el Ashrâf el Khalîl after his conquest of Acre in 1291.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
View of the great sea from Athlît. Through a large pointed arch, which is only held in position by the extreme hardness and tenacity of the cement used in construction of this fortress.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Remains of a crusading fort at Tantûrah. Its shattered tower is thirty feet in height.  In the distance the village of Tantûrah appears, in the site of the ancient city of Dor.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The castle of Caesarea. A medieval structure, with marble columns built transversely into the walls. In the interior there are several vaulted chambers.  It stands on the ancient mole on the south side of the harbour.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Columns in the sea, Caesarea, formed of granite and various kinds of marble; they are relics of Herod's city which were used by medieval builders to strengthen sea walls which have now perished.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Part of the north wall and moat of Caesarea.  The walls are six feet in thickness and are strengthened by buttresses; they are still from twenty to thirty feet in height.  The moat is lined with masonry.  There are three ruined towers in the north wall, two of which are shown above.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
Tower of the castle at Caeserea. Built by the crusaders.  It probably occupies the site of "Strato's tower," which was succeeded by the "Tower Drusus" of Herod.

Remains of a fortified khan at Mukhâlid. A saracenic structure, which has long  been in ruins.  It  is nearly a mile from the seashore and close to the little village of Mukhâlid.  The solitary tree near to it is a well-known landmark.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Neby ben Yamîn (Tomb of the prophet Benjamin).  A Mohammaden shrine about half a mile to the east of Kefr Saba. A well of good water adjoins it.  In the foreground a peasant is guiding a primitive plough and a yoke of oxen.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Kefar Saba.  A straggling village consisting of houses built chiefly of sun-dried bricks, with extensive orchards to the west and south of it.  It is fourteen miles from Jaffa, and is interesting in as much as it preserves the name of the ancient Caphar Saba.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Johnstone, J.

The castle of Mirabel.  Now called Kûlat Râs el 'Ain, built by the Crusaders before the year 1149.  It is nor a mere shell and encloses a large space of ground, in the centre of which stands a small mosque.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The Nahr el Aujeh from Kûlat Râs el 'Ain.  The river rises out of the earth in several copious streams at the foot of the mound on which the castle stands.  This mound has been satisfactorily identified as the site of Antipatris.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
Sacred tree called Sheikh et Teim. South of the extensive mound of ruins and tombs known to the Arabs as Tibneh, but which has long  been regarded as the site of Tinmath Sera, the city of Joshua.
The traditional tomb of Joshua, in the rock cemetary at Tibneh.  In the niches of its walls pilgrims placed lighted lamps, and in their great number indicates that it was a highly revered shrine.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Joshua (Biblical figure)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Armytage, James Charles (d. 1897)

Landing at Jaffa. This is always attended with difficulty, as there is no harbor for large vessels at Jaffa.  Steamers are obliged to anchor in the roadstead, about half a mile from the shore, and passengers are landed in small Arab boats.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The mosque at Jaffa.  A modern structure in the north-east quarter of the town.  It can easily be distinguished in the general view of Jaffa (see steel plate). where it appears between the masts of the Arab fishing boats.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
Shittim tree at Jaffa, in the Mohammadan cemetary north of the town, close to the sea.  Represented at the hour of sunset, the time of evening prayer.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The traditional house of Simon the Tanner.  A Mohammadan sanctuary.  On the south side of the court of the house there is an arched recess, in which a lamp is always kept burning, and where pilgrims perform their devotions.  A well of good water and a fig tree add to the attractiveness of this 'place'.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

View of the rock-encircled harbour at Jaffa, from the roof of the house of Simon the Tanner.  The building in the foreground, with its domes and perforated parapets, is a characteristic example of native domestic architecture in towns and cities of Southern Palestine.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
A roadside fountain and tomb.  The Sebîl of Abû Nabût, commonly called the Tomb of Tabitha (Dorcas).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
Public fountain at Jaffa, near to the gate of the town, shaded by an octagonal domed structure, formed of eight pointed arches supported by columns.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Scene in a Jaffa garden.  Two women engaged in working a sâkiyeh, a clumsy machine for raising water from a well to fill a reservoir.  On the branch of the pomegranate there is a chameleon.

Scene in the bazaar at Jaffa.  A public café, in a deep arched recess, with a group of smokers.  An attendant pounding coffee is steadying a wooden mortar with his naked feet. In the foreground there are fruit-stalls and a Bedouin with his tufted lance; a water-carrier and a peasant boy leading a camel are passing by.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Sanctuary of Imâm 'Aly.  Surmounted on one large and eight smaller domes.  On the road between Jaffa and Ramleh, near the village of Yazûr.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Crew, John J.

The tower at Ramleh. Said to be the minaret of a large mosque which once stood here.  According to an Arabic inscription over the door, it was built in the year 1318.  It is known as the White Mosque.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Ruins of the church of St. George at Ludd, the ancient Lydda.  The nave and the north aisle have recently been converted into a Greek church; the south aisle is destroyed, and the remainder is used as the court of a mosque.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Plain of Sharon from the tower, Ramleh.  This tower, shown on page 144, was the minaret of a mosque called Jâmi'a el Abtad. It has a winding staircase of one hundred and twenty steps.  Its eastern windows overlook the town of Ramleh and the plain beyond, bounded by the hills of Judea.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Sur'ah, the ancient Zorah.  The birthplace of Sampson.  It is five miles south of Latrôn, on a conical hill on the north side of the Wâdy es Sur'ar (The valley of Sorek).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley

The ruined fortress of Latrôn, from 'Amwâs, the Emmaus of the Maccabees, afterwards called Nicopolis.  In the foreground are the remains of the ancient church of Emmaus. There is a direct road, running southwards, from  Latrôn to Zorah, over hills dotted with ruined sites.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Shrine of Sheikh Samat at Sur'ah (Zorah), on the summit of the hill. Below is shown the upper part of the Wâdy es Su'ar (Vally of Sorek), which falls into the river called Nahr Rubîn.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Badoureau, Ed.

'Ain Shems, the site of Beth-Shemesh.  South of the Wâdy es Sur'ar (Sorek) and nearly opposite to Sur'ah (Zorah).  The ancient and modern names Beth-Shemesh (House of the Sun) and 'Ain Shems (Eye of the Sun) are indicative of sun worship.
The valley of Sorek.  Where the men of Beth-Shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest when the ark arrived from Ekron.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)
Tibneh, the site of Timnath.  The home of Samson's wife , and the scene of his encounter with the young lion in the vineyard.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Harley
Wâdy es Sunt, the Valley of Elah.   The scene of David's encounter with Goliath.  THe valley winds between the low hills and enters the plain of Philistia opposite Tel es Sâfy.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); David, King of Israel
Shocoh, the camp of the Philistines.  This site, now called Shuweikeh, is marked by extensive ruins, large terebinth-trees, and a Mohammadan shrine dedicated to Sheikh Abû Helâl.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Ploughing in the plains of Philistia, in the neighborhood of Tell es Sâfy. Ploughing and sowing for winter crops extends from the end of November to the middle of January or later.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Tell es Sâfy, the supposed site of Gath. An isolated hill of irregular form sixteen miles from the seashore.  A shrine dedicated to El Khudr (St. George) stands on the highest point, six hundred and ninety-three feet above the sea.  The Roman road runs north and south on the eastern side of the Tell.

Yabneh, the ancient Jabneh. Called also Jabneel, and by the Greeks Jamnia.  It is a large village, four miles from the seashore, surrounded by orchards. Its mosque was once a Christian church. Its port, once the rival of Joppa, has now almost entirely disappeared.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Eshdûd, the ancient Ashdod.  Called by the Greeks Azotus.  The modern village stands on the slope of a hill, one hundred feet above the sea, and three miles from the shore.  The green knoll in the foreground is crowned by the wely of Sheikh Ibrahim el Matbûk.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
El Mejdel, the Ancient Migdol.  An important village of fifteen hundred inhabitants.  Its mosque and tall minaret are constructed of ancient materials. A weekly fair is held here.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Ruins of Ascalon, from the North-east. Here there are fine orchards and olive- trees, cultivated by the Egyptian peasants of the neighboring village of El Jûrah. The wild onions of 'Askûlon are celebrated for their delicate flavor. The Romans gave them the name of Ascalonia, hence scalogn (Ital.) and shallot (Allium Ascalonicum).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Willmore, Arthur (1814-1888); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Ruins of Ashkelon, from the South-west.  Here there is a shallow bay, with a landing-place for small boats.  The beach is strewn with masses of ancient masonry. On the cliff above there is a Mohammadan shrine, called El Khudrah, with a few palm trees near it.

Ruins of Ashkelon, from the North.  Showing fortifications at the north-west corner of the city.  The western wall was about twelve hundred feet in length and followed the lines of the edge of the cliffs which are from thirty to seventy feet in height. The conquest of Ascalon by Rameses II is recorded on the walls of the Temple of Karnac.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Güzzeh, the ancient Gaza.  The modern village, which is of semi-Egyptian character, has neither walls nor gates. The serai dates from the thirteenth century, and the great mosque, Jami'a el Kebîr, which towers above the palm trees, was originally a Byzantine cathedral.
A well in the plain of Philistia. Around it there were a few rudely formed cup-shaped stone water-troughs for the use of flocks and herds.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The castle of Beir Jibrîn, by starlight.  Arab musicians in the foreground. The one stringed instrument is the 'rabâb esh shâ'ir' or poet's viol; it is used as an accompaniment to chanted poetry. The double-reed pipe is the 'arghûl;' its longer reed serves as a drone or continuous bass.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Subterranean labyrinth of Tell Sandannah (Beit Jibrin). Showing on of the numerous circular dome-shaped caverns, with its winding rock-cut stairway.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)

The Valley of Beit Jibrîn. With a distant view of the sea and sandy coast hills.  On the hillside on the left the entrance to one of the great caverns with which this district abounds is shown.  In the foreground a shepherd is sleeping; near to him are his dog and gun and double-reed pipe.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The church of Saint Anne, Beit Jibrîn. Called by the Arabs El Kenîseh ; it stands at one thousand and seventy two feet above the sea, opposite to Tell Sandannah (Santa Hanna?). It was originally a Byzantine church, but was restored by the Crusaders.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Anne (Mother of the Virgin Mary), Saint
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Krausse, Alfred

Valley of Berachah.  Jehosaphat's 'valley of blessing.' A wide open vale between Tekoa and the road from Hebron to Bethlehem. In the foreground there is a lime-kiln, and on the distant hill a ruined site, two thousand eight hundred and fifeen feet above the sea, called Khurbet Bereikuh.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The wilderness of Judea. With a view of the Dead Sea (Bahr Lût) and the mountains of Moab at sunrise.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Teku'a, the site of Tekoa. Showing the remains of a Byzantine church, and its massive baptismal font of octagonal form.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Râmat el Khulîl, the sight of Mamre. The camping place of Abraham.  It is a little way to the right of the old Roman road to Jerusalem, and is also known as Beit Khulîl, "the house of Abraham."
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Wâdy et Tuffâh, commonly called the vale of Eschol. The peasants grouped in the foreground are under the southern branches  of Abraham's oak. In the distance the minaret of the great mosque of Sheikh 'Ali Bakka, Hebron, may be distinguished.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Abraham's Oak, Hebron.  An ilex or evergreen holm oak (quercus pseudo-cocccifera). One of the lower branches was broken down by a heavy fall of snow in the winter of 1850.  It was cut up into logs and conveyed to Jerusalem. There were seven camel loads; one log was sent to England.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Abraham (Biblical patriarch)

The pools of Hebron.  The chief pool is one hundred and thirty-two feet square, and twenty-one feet deep. There are stone steps leading to the bottom at each corner.  The other pool is eight-four feet in length and fifty-four feet in width.  The enclosed building in the distance, on the slope of the hill to the left, is the Quarantine station.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Ruined wely, Hebron.  On the rocky heights south of the city. Beyond the cemetary and the olive groves the Hâret esh Sheikh, the northern quarter of Hebron, appears.

The Dead Sea, looking north-east from Engedi.  Anciently called the Salt Sea and the Sea of the Plain.  The name Dead Sea, now so familiar, does not occur in the Bible ; it was adopted by Greek and Roman writers in the second century of our era.  The Arabs call this sea Bahr Lût (Sea of Lot.)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Badoureau, Ed.
The mountains of Moab from Engedi.  At this point the Dead Sea is about nine miles in width. There is a continuous beach of varying breadth along the shore.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Engedi, the fountain of the Kid ('Ain Jidy). The sparkling limpid water is warm, rather sweet and impregnated with lime.  To the left there is an example of the remarkable esclepiad called in Arabic 'osher ; it bears a bladder-like fruit filled with long silky hairs, used by Arabs as tinder for their matchlocks.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Badoureau, Ed.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Southern end of the Dead Sea from Engedi.  Showing the peninsula called El Lisân (the tongue) which may easily be mistaken for an island.

The cliffs of Engedi.  They form an very difficult pass, and the zigzag paths are not kept in repair.  The surface of the limestone rock is of marble-like smoothness, and a pale reddish tint is the prevailing color.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The wilderness of Engedi, where David and his followers lived among the 'rocks of the wild goats'. There are many caves in the hillside which might well serve as a place of refuge for fugitives and outlaws.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Bîr es Seba': the site of Beersheba.  The ancient wells can still be traced, and two of them are serviceable ; but the city has ceased to exist.  In the distance may be seen an encampment of the Tiyâheh Arabs.  In the foreground a woman is asking  alms...
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Harley
'Ain el Weibeh, on the border of Edom, in the valley of El Jeib.  The name signifies "hole with water.: Many authorities regard this now deserted place as the site of Kadesh Barnea.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Rock-cut tomb or temple, Petra. Eighty-five feet in height. It is called by the Arabs El Khuzneh Far'on, 'The treasures of Pharoah,' which is said to be concealed in the urn-shaped finial at the summit. The portal leads into a lofty chamber twelve yards square.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Detached tombs, Petra.  Isolated masses of rock, from fifteen to twenty feet square.  In one of them there is a small sepulchral chamber.  The background represents the excavations in the cliffs opposite to the amphitheatre.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The rock-hewn amphitheatre, Petra. Thirty-three tiers of seats rise one above the other, and above the seats there are chambers hewn in rock.  The brook of 'Ain Mûsa, bordered with verdure, flows across the arena.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)
Entrance to the valley of Petra
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Bertrand, C. (fl. 188-)
Mount Hor. The scene of the death of Aaron, called by the Arabs Jebel Harûn, "the Mount of Aaron." Its highest point is about four thousand three hundred and sixty feet above the sea level.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Rock-cut tombs, Petra.  Used as dwelling houses by local tribes in cold or wet weather.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Cliffs of the Sîk, Petra.  Showing the western outlet of the great defile opposite to the rock-cut amphitheatre represented on page 216.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Dier, Petra. An isolated building on a lofty eminence north-west of the valley of Petra.  It faces Mount Hor.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Jezîrat Far'on, the Isle of Pharaoh.  At the head of the Gulf of 'Akabah, as seen from the western shore.  The castle which crowns it was built by the Crusaders; the mosque and other Saracenic structures are attributed to Saladin.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Letter of admission to the convent of St. Catherine.  Formerly travellers were drawn up into the convent through the pent-house shown above; now however, if a letter thus received is found satisfactory they are admitted by a side door.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Saint Catherine (Monastery : Mount Sinai)

A peep into one of the courts of the convent. Showing a rude flight of steps leading to the upper chambers.  On the left the summits of the belfry of the church and the minaret of the mosque may be seen.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Saint Catherine (Monastery : Mount Sinai)
The upper chambers of the convent.  With the peaks of Jebel Mûsa in the background.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Saint Catherine (Monastery : Mount Sinai)

View from the north-eastern galleries. Showing the lofty chamber of the south corner, A monk at a lower window is striking a piece of suspended iron with a hammer, to call the fraternity to prayers in one of the numerous chapels.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Saint Catherine (Monastery : Mount Sinai)

Interior of the church of the convent of Saint Catherine.  The framework of the door leading into the nave is richly decorated ; its panels are embellished with enamels. From the ceiling hang numerous silver lamps and ostrich eggs suspended by long cord.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Saint Catherine (Monastery : Mount Sinai)

The crescent and the cross. The belfry of the church and the minaret of the mosque,  standing so near to each other within convent walls, produce a singular effect. and strange to say the former is of recent construction, while the latter dates from an earlier period.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Quartley, Frederick William (1808-1874)
Gate of St. Stephen the Porter.  An archway on the assent to Jebel Mûsa. where pilgrims formerly confessed before they visited the sacred heights.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Well in the garden of the convent of St. Catherine. This garden is north-west of the convent, and is enclosed by a high wall.  The lofty chamber at the north corner of the convent is shown above.
Eastern tower of the convent of Saint Catherine, and part of the convent garden, with the plain of Er Râhah and the narrow pass called Nukb Hâwy in the distance.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Saint Catherine (Monastery : Mount Sinai)
Râs Atâkah. Râs is the same as our "nase" or "naze."  This bold promontory. south of Suez, running out from Jebel Atâkah, on the western shore of the Red Sea, comes into every view of Suez.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Under the palms, 'Ayun Músa. 'It is a strange spot- this plot of tamarisks' (and palms) 'with its seventeen wells - literally an island in the desert and now used as the Richmond of Suez- a comparison which chiefly serves to show what a place Suez itself must be!'  -- (Stanley)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Gulf of Suez, looking out from 'Ayún Músa. These complicated wheels and spars are a mixture of Egyptian shádoof and sâkiyeh (water-wheel), by which the precious water is raised from the wells.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
'Ayún Músa.  From this spot one probably commences the real desert journey.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Red Sea, as seen during the first day's march in the desert.  The proper adjustment of the load of the camel's back requires much skill. If it is unevenly balanced the poor beast suffers a good deal and begins grumbling until things are made ship-shape.
A halt in the desert. The Bedawin never trouble themselves with tents when on a journey.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
In the wilderness of Shur. A small encampment of Bedawin, probably of the Terabin tribe, whose territory extends as far as Gaza.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Sand-storm in the desert. The dreaded khamseen (wind and sand storm) very frequently overtakes the traveller in the region between 'Ayún Músa and Wâdy Amârah.  Dean Stanley, Neibhur, Miss Martineau all encountered it here.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
'Ain Hawwârah. This may be the spring "Marah" of Exodus xv.23.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Wâdy Amârah.  Of Wâdy Amârah, some forty miles away from Ayún Músa, Professor Palmer says, 'There is no other water but this (at Bir Abu Suweirah, twelve miles distant) in or near Wâdy Amârah.' A proof that this wâdy is not to be identified with the Marah of the Bible.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The springs in Wâdy Gharandel, probably the "Elim" of the Bible.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The cliffs of Jebel Hammâm Farún. The altitude given in the "Ordinance survey map" for Jebel Hammâm Farún is 1,567 feet.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Jebel Hammâm Farún. The hot springs bubble up at intervals from the sand, and also issue from several features in the rocks.  The temperature of the water is 160º.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Rock foms in Wâdy Hamr. This valley leads up to Jebel et Tih.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)
Wâdy Useit. One can go down to the sea-shore by this valley, but the path is hardly passable for camels.  There are clumps of stunted palms every here and there, and some brackish water.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wâdy Taiyebeh. "The valley of good" (water and pasture). Through this valley most probably the Israelites journeyed to their encampment by the Red Sea.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Wâdy Taiyebeh, with the Red Sea in sight,  The lower part of the valley is very picturesque.  The horizontal strata of the cliffs and their bright coloring make a deep impression on one from the desert.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The plain El  Markeiyeh. At the mouth of Wâdy Taiyebeh, looking south and south-east towards the mountains of the Serbál group.  The plain takes its name from the long white range of chalk hills called El Markhâ.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Near the mouth of the Wâdy Taibeiyeh, looking north west.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Râs Abu Zenimeh. On a low promontory running out somewhat farther into the sea is placed the tomb of the saint.  Unless it is rough the camels are made to take to the water instead of climbing the cliffs.
Jebel el Markhâ. This ridge of limestone, about nine hundred feet high, separates the two plains of El Markheyeh and El Markhâ.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
The plain of El Markhâ. This weary plain of flinty barenness slopes gently to the sea, the glare from which and from the limestone cliff is almost overpowering.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Rocks in the ravine of Sarâbit el Khâdim. And a natural gallery in the same ravine.  Wind and storm have worn these sandstone rocks into the most fantastic shapes.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Badoureau, Ed.
The stelae and ruins at Sârabít el Khâdim.  The latest of these stelae date from Ramese IV, of the twentieth century.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)

The rocks at Sarâbít el Khâdim ; and the temple enclosure. There are two temples, of different dates.  The one not shown here is formed of two chambers excavated in the rock, having a walled continuation in front.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Brandard, Edward Paxman (1819-1898); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wâdy Sidreh. The Wâdies Mukatteb, Sidreh and Igné all debouch into the Seib Sidreh.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
The road up Nagb Buderah. By this pass travellers usually approach Mukatteb from Egypt.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913)
The outlet of Wâdy Nagb Buderah, in the Seih Sidreh. The Acacia seyal is the shittah or shittim tree of the Bible.  The "seyal" is the only timber tree of any size in the Arabian desert.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wâdy Shellâl, "Vally of the Cataracts." This valley bears, both in name and aspect, ever trace of wintery cascades.  It leads up to the pass of Nagb Buderah.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
Views from the tourquoise mines of Maghârah.  Wâdy Maghârah is another name for Wâdy Igné (properly Gena). The mines are high up on the left side as one ascends the narrow wâdy.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The cliffs, mines and Egyptian tablets of Maghârah.  These mines were worked more than four thousand years ago.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wâdy Mukhateb, the "written valley" or "valley of inscriptions." The celebrated Sinaitic inscriptions abound in this valley on the right-hand side as one passes down.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Cousen, Charles (1819-1889); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Wâdy Mukatteb.  The strange shapes of the weather-worn sandstone rocks are almost as noteworthy as the Sinaitic inscriptions.  In the inscriptions represented in this illustration the camel occurs frequently.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wâdy Feirân.  The rock supposed to have been struck by Moses is in the right-hand forground.  The Arabs call it Hesy el Khattatin.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Jebel el Benât, "Girls Mountain." Stands some seven miles to the north of Serbâl.
Wâdy Feirân. Acacia seyal is the same as the shittim-tree.  The Arabs lop these trees for charcoal, &c., in the cruellest and most unscientific manner.
Jebel Tâhúneh, the "Mountiain of the windmill." Opposite Serbâl, on the north side of the Feirân valley.  The ruined city Pheran, or Feiran, lies at its foot.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
A spring in Wâdy Feirân.  To the Bedawin of Sinai, Feirân realizes paradise.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Bradshaw, Samuel, engraver
Wâdy Feirân. Professor Palmer describes the walk through Wâdy Feirân, with its shade of palms, tamarisksm and sidr-trees, and with its running water, as one of the most delightful in Sinai.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
