'El Maharrad,' Pharan (Feirân). These ruins are all that remain of the great church and old monastic establishment of Pharan. The Bedawin grow small patches of maize, bearded wheat, and tobacco about here.
Tamarisk- tree, Wâdy Feirân, Sinai.  "And the sleep in the dried river channel, where bulrushes tell/ That the water was wont to go warbling so softly and well." -- Browining's "Saul."
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Badoureau, Ed.

Alluvial desposits, Wâdy Feirân.  These strange deposits serve as a "meter" to measure the height to which the Feirân streams may once have reached.  At Philae, &c., in the valley of the Nile, the same deposits may be observed.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
El Buwieb, the "gate" of Feirân.  A narrow passage between the rocks, about one hundred feet by twenty long.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Beidhat umm Tâkhah, a neighbor of Mount Serbál.  In the foreground is the usual scene of preparation for a night's bivouac.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Tarfah or tamarisk grove, Wâdy es Sheikh. This fine grove is called Tarfat el Gidarin.  The wâdy itself cuts through the granite wall which fences in Sinai.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Hajar el Lagweh, "The speaking stone." A rock covered with Sinaitic inscriptions in Wâdy Berrah, "The valley of the passer-out." From this valley you pass into a more open country and leave the sandstone district.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Magâd en Nebí Músa, 'Seat of the prophet Moses.' This large detached rock, which from one point looks something like an arm-chair, occurs in the gorge of El Watiyeh. Near here is pointed out the place where Moses' sheep grazed.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

A recollection of Sinai and the mountains of the pass of the wind.  "On Horeb, with Elijah, let us lie/ Where all around, on mountain, sand, and sky,/ God's chariot-wheels have left distinctest trace." -- Keble.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Arabs.  These Arabs are Towarah, who generally prefer turban and fez to gailey - striped kefiyeh.  One of them has in his hand the head of an ibex (bedan).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wâdy Sh'reich. One of the peaks in the Wâdy Sh'reich is called Jebel Abu Mahrúreh, "The thunder-stricken mountain," a large portion of its summit having been detached by a thunderbolt.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Near the mouth of Wâdy Sh'reich. The scene of the worship of the golden calf was placed by early tradition at the mouth of this valley.
Wâdy T'lâh, Mount Sinai. This wâdy runs parallel with the plain Er Râhah. but flows in a contrary direction.  It is marvellously beautiful and picturesque.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
Wâdy Katarína, Sinai. This rocky glen, which goes by the name Shagg Músa, leads up from the orchards and gardens of the Convent of El Arab'in.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Cliffs of Jebel Katarína.  Of the three peaks of the Jebel Katarina cluster, Jebel Zebir is the central.  Jebel Katarina lies half a mile to the north of it; and Jebal Abu Rumail a mile to the south.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Cousen, Charles (1819-1889)

Convent of the Arba'in (of the forty), Wâdy Lejâ.  The situation of this convent is most secluded and picturesque.  The celebrated 'Moses' Rock' loses its claim to notoriety, if Rephidim be located in Wâdy Feirán.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Mountains at the head of Wâdy Lejâ.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Gardens near the mouth of Wâdy Lejâ.  The winding road seen in the cliffs leads up to Jebel Tiniyeh, where are the remains of the half-finished palace of the late 'Abbas Pasha.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Bedawín encampment, Wâdy Sebíyeh, Sinai. This valley has been  mentioned as a likely camping ground for the Israelites, because of the view afforded of the summit of Jebel Músa.  There is no open space, however, for a great multitude.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Johnstone, J.
Jebel Músa from the south, Sinai.  Wâdy Seba'iyeh, through which the way passes from Jebel Umm Shomer, offers the traveller a splendid view of the steep southern extremity of Jebel Músa.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The chapel and grotto of Elijah, Jebel Músa. This gigantic cypress is one of the world-famous trees. In Niebuhr's time there were two of them.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
Looking east from Râs Sufsâfeh, Sinai.  In the smaller illustration is represented the summit of Jebel Mûsa, with the chapel and less conspicuous mosque.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Palmer, William James
Ma'yan Músa, the spring of Moses, Sinai.  At this spring, rising up in a cool shady rock-grotto, the Bedawin believe Moses to have watered Jethro's rocks.

Jebel Sûna, from Sikket Syednâ Músa, "The path of our lord Moses." The path is very steep and difficult ; it reaches the basin at the back of Râs Sufsâfeh after a climb of one thousand five hundred feet.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
Âs Sufsâfeh (Mount Sinai) and the plain of Râhah (Rest).  Beyond the convent is seen Jebel Moneijâh. The summit of Jebel Músa is hidden behind the overwelming mass of Râs Sufsâfeh.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)

Defile of the Jebel Tíh.  The long white range of the Tíh mountains, mostly of the same average height, forms the southern and south-eastern boundary of the great 'wilderness of the forty year's wanderings.'
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Suez.  The approach to the Suez canal from the south is by an artificially deepened channel in the gulf.  A stone pier one mile and three-quarters in length, erected on a sand-bank, runs from Suez to the entrance of this channel.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Lake Timsâh, midway in the Suez Canal.  It is traversed by two artificial channels for the passage of large vessels.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Mahsamah.  In the Wâdy Tûmîlât, between Tell-el-Maskhûtah (Pithom) and  Tell-el-Kebîr.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

A village threshing floor.  Showing a primitive threshing-sledge drawn by buffaloes, and a peasant separating the chaff from the grain with a winnowing fork.  The huts of the village are formed of mud and sun-dried bricks, roofed with palm tree rafters thatched with stalks of Indian corn, palm leaves, and old mats.  The dark patches on the mud walls represent cakes of fuel made of dung and straw ; when thoroughly dry they are stored for use.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
Brickmaking.  A wooden frame is placed in position, ready to receive the clay.
A wayside well. Shaded by a fine specimen of the Acacia Nilotica.  The water is raised by means of jars attached to a wheel, the sâkiyeh.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Obelisk of Heliopolis. Formed of red granite ; it has been so much encroached upon by deposits of mud that a considerable portion of its base is now covered.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The "Virgin's tree."  At the time of the inauguration of the Suez Canal this tree was presented to the Empress Eugénie by the Khedive.  The garden in which it stands is watered by means of a double sakîyeh supplied from a reservoir fed by springs.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Johnstone, J.
The gate of victory. (Bâb-en-Nasr).  The easternmost of the northern gates of Cairo. It was built in the reign of the Fâtimy khalif El-Mustansir, A.H. 480 (A.D. 1087).

A seller of lanterns.  In houses provided with latticed windows only, candles are usually sheltered by lanterns like those suspended above.  One such lantern, with two or three wax candles in it, placed on the ground or on a low stool in a central position, is considered sufficient to light a large saloon.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Sebîl, or street fountain.  Supplied from a cistern below which is filled during the inundation of the Nile.  The upper chamber, with its columns and double veranda, is a school-room.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Carpet bazaar.  There are two carpet bazaars in the Khân-El-Khalîly. The larger one is established in the picturesque court of a cuilding of the thirteenth century, a portion of which is shown above.  Here may be seen carpets from India and Persia and from every part of the Turkish empire.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
In the shoe bazaar. This was formerly a school, an interesting building now in a very dilapadated condition. The gateway, however, is still preserved.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The armourer's market.  In this street, there are some good specimens of meshrebíehs (latticed windows).
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Tomb- mosque of El- Ashraf Barsabay.  In the Eastern Cemetary, or so-called "Tomb of the Khalifs."  It is constructed of alternate courses of pale red and yellowish white limestone.  Barsabay died A.D. 1438
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
Fountains in the court of the mosque of Sultan Hasan.  The recess beyond it on the eastern side of the court is the sanctuary.  The arch is ninety feet in height.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Lauderbach, James W.

Court of the tomb-mosque of Barkûk.  In the Eastern Cemetary.  A fountain for ablution, shaded by two trees, stands in the centre of the court, which is surrounded by a colonnade.  The sanctuary occupies the space between two fine domes, one of which is shown above.  Barkûk died in A.D. 1399.
Pulpit of the tomb-mosque of Barkûk.  Presented by the Kaït Bay.  It is  carved of hard limestone, and is one of the most beautiful existing specimens of Arabian sculpture.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

At school.  Small wooden boards painted white serve instead of books, the lessons being written on them in ink by the schoolmaster, and renewed from time to time.  The children, seated on the floor, read or recite the appointed lesson all at once, while rocking themselves to and fro or swaying from side to side.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Tomb-mosque of Kaît Bay.  In the Eastern Cemetary.  It is constructed of alternate courses of pale red and yellowish white limestone.  Kaît Bay died A.D. 1496.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Hartley, J. Q.; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Valley of the Nile and pyramids.  From Mount Mukattam.  Beyond the picturesque cluster of the "Tomb of the Memlûks" we see the ancient aqueduct stretching across the mounds of rubbish which form the southern moundary of Cairo.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The citadel from the "Tombs of the Memlûks."  The Great Mosque of Mohammed 'Aly with is tall minarets and clister of somes dtands within the Citadel, and is the most conspicuous land-mark of Cairo.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
One of the 'Tombs of the Memlûks.' On Mount Mukattam. In the foreground is the musattah, or camel-litter, ordinarily used by pilgrims.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Meeder, Philip (d. 1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Tombs of the Memlûks." The whole of this region is dotted with gravestones and is still used as a burial ground.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Mosques on Mukattam. Caverns and quarries are numerous on the slopes of the Mukattam hills, which are of nummulite foundation and extremely rich in fossils.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
On the canal (El Khalîg). Ths water-way, which runs through Cairo, was formerly navigable at high Nile.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Cooper, J. (fl. 19th cent.); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

A water-wheel (sâkiyeh) on the canal.  When the creaking wooden wheels are in motion the earthenware jars, strung to ropes made of palm fibre, revolve, alternately dripping into the water and emptying themselves into a trough connected with a reservoir.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Saddler, John (1813-1892); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

In a Cairo garden.  Where the date-palm, the Cactus optunia, almond-trees, acacias, and sycamores, the common trees of the country, flourish.  During the reign of the Khedive Isma'îl about two hundred different kinds of trees, chiefly of East Indian origin, were planted in great numbers in the new parks and gardens of Cairo.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

A suburban cafe.  the two men on the bench in the foreground are playing a game called mankalah; small pebbles are placed, according to certain rules, in hemispherical holes in a board.  This game exercises the powers of calculation; and it is often played at cafes.  The loser is expected to pay not only for the coffee drunk by himself and his antagonist, but by the spectators of the game.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Street in Masr El-Atîkah. The man in the foreground is selling water flavored with orange blossom.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Bazaar in Bûlâk.  Bûlâk is the river harbor of Cairo ; here goods from Upper Egypt, Nubia, and central Africa are landed, and the bazaars are often crowded with natives of distant provinces during the busy season.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
View from the top of the Great Pyramid
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Village barbers. The two singular structures on the left are pigeon-houses. The domes are formed of earthen pots of oval form ; each pair of pigeons occupies a separate pot.  These birds are kept solely for the sake of the manure they yield.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Orr, Nathaniel
The Sphinx. Called by the Arabs "Father of terrors." It faces the east, and is hewn out of the natural rock.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The fallen statue of Rameses II at Memphis.  The soft mud in which it is embedded has perfectly preserved the well-cut features and all the front part of the figure.  During about eight months of the year it is partly covered by the waters of the overflowing Nile.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Ramses II, King of Egypt
The Pyramid of Steps at Sakkârah.  Constructed of an inferior clayey kind of limestone quarried in the neighborhood.  Possibly the oldest monument in Egypt.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)
The pyramid of Meydûm.  The Arabs call it "The False Pyramid." Its outer walls consist of admirably jointed and polished blocks of Mukattam stone. The base is hidden by a heap of debris.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Tomb of a Muslim saint at Minyeh.  Shaded by an ancient sycamore-tree.  It is on the north side of the town, near to the spot where boats are generally moored.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
View of the Nile from the tombs of Beny Hasan. These grottos, the interior of one of which is also shown, were excavated by a single family of the time of the Twelfth Dynasty.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The gateway of Asyût. It opens into a large gateway court which forms part of the governor's palace and leads into the town.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The necropolis of Asyût, consisting of ancient rock-tombs and a modern cemetary (to the right), approached from the town by a bridge over a canal which skirts the cultivated land.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Pigeon-towers on the Nile. The battlements are formed of earthenware pots, and rows of Indian corn stalks project from the loopholed walls to serve as perches.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
A silhouette on the Nile.  A group of the slate colored buffaloes of the country being watered is one of the commonest sights on the Nile.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Girgeh, from the mooring-place on the south side.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913)

Shadûf. The weight of the water in the bucket is balanced by the lump of Nile mud at the other end of the swinging beam, and the water is thus raised to the mouth of the canal with little effort; but pulling the bucket down is hard work, and the machine is ruinously extravagant in labour.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
A Ptolemaic temple, dedicated to the goddess Hathor, the Egyptian Aphrodite, and famous for its portaits of Cleopatra.

The plain of Thebes from near Karnak.  In the foreground is seen a modern saint's tomb in the middle-distance, the lateen sails of the Nile boats, the twin Colossi, and the Ramesêum stand out above the river, and the view is closed by the finest mountain in Egypt, whose steep ships are honeycombed with tombs, and whose towering mass guards and conceals the gloomy "Valley of the Kings" behind.
The Valley of the Tombs of the Kings. The interior of one of the tombs, dimly lighted by those torches wherewith travellers blacken and destroy monuments, is shown beneath.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The Ramesêum. The remains of the great hypostyle of the Temple of Rameses II.  The figures of Christian slaves have been painted on some of the columns.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Ramses II, King of Egypt

The vocal Memnon.  The nearer colossus formerly gave forth a low sound when the rays of the rising sun first glanced upon it.  The "song of Memnon" was famous in Roman times and is even said to have been heard in the present century.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Amenhotep III, King of Egypt
Pylon of the temple of Thothmes III. At Medînet Habû.  Commonly called the small temple, in contradistinction to its greater neighbour. It has been restored and added to in Ptolomaic and Roman times.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Thutmose III, King of Egypt

The court of the great temple of Rameses III. At Medînet Habû.  The short pillars in front belonged to the church which the Copts erected within this noble peristyle court, and of which many other columns strew the ground.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Ramses III, King of Egypt
The mosque of Luxor. Ornamented in black upon a white-washed ground in the manner characteristic of Upper Egypt.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The obelisk of Luxor.  The hieroglyphics are cleanly and deeply cut in the red granite.  The fellow of this monolith has been carried away to Paris, and set up in the Place de la Concorde.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Godfrey, John (ca. 1817-1889)

Niche in an ancient Christian church, Luxor. Part of the temple of Amenoph III, converted into a church.  Frescoes, of some pretentions to artistic merit, half cover the ancient bas-reliefs ; and the figures of Egyptian gods mingle eccentrically with the aureoles of Christian saints.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
The gate of Ptolemy Euergetes, Karnak.  Showing the pylon of the Temple of Khons beyond.  An avenue of rams leads up to this beautiful gate, which is the most gracely of all the structures at Karnak.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Ptolemy III Euergetes, King of Egypt, d. 221 B.C.

The smaller obelisk of Karnak.  Belonging to the pylon of Thomthmes I.  The fragments of a fellow obelisk strew the ground.  Behind is seen the central avenue of the Hall of Columns, and the clerestory windows are shown at the left-hand side.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

The leaning column, Karnak. In one side of the aisles of the Hall of Columns. The base is worn and the foundations undermined by the Nile, which at the inundation rises some six feet above the level of the floor.
Grand column of Karnak. At the west entrance to the Hall of Columns.  The central avenue is here seen from the opposite end to that shown on the engraving on page 449.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Armytage, James Charles (d. 1897)
The Nile, from Luxor. The two women in the foreground wear the ordinary black burko', or veil, joined to the head-dress by a piece of cane placed between the eyes.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The Dôm palm.  Groups of these eccentric-looking trees form a characteristic feature of the scenery of upper Egypt.  They are not found south of the Thebaïd.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Temple of Edfû.  The towers of the great pylon are one hundred and twenty feet high, and in almost perfect preservation.  The columns of the hypostyle hall are seen over the wall of the enclosure, which springs from the pylon and runs around the whole building.
Doorway of a side chapel of the temple of Edfû.  After leaving this chapel the priestly procession ascended the winding stone staircase opposite, which conducts by a series of easy steps to the roof.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Cousen, Charles (1819-1889); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

Rock tombs or Gebel-es-Silsileh.  At this point the Nile is scarcely eleven hundred feet wide.  The rocky barrier through which the river has forced its way is honeycombed with grottoes of the time of the great Theban dynasties.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Filmer, John; Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Distant view of Kom Ombo.  The fine Ptolemaic temple stands out boldly on the edge of the cliff, over which it is gradually falling in a cascade of white masonry.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

Aswân, the Syene of Juvenal.  The chief entrance to the town is beneath the two noble lebbekh trees to the left of the minaret, and opposite the landing place for streamers.  Dahabîyehs moor higher up, as is shown in the foreground.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The temple of Kom Ombo,  Half buried in sand-drifts, and half fallen over the river bank, the temple of Kom Ombo is one of the lonliest, and, at a distance, the most impressive of the smaller shrines of Egypt.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Badoureau, Ed.; Temple of Sobek and Haroeris (Ombos)

On the island of Elephantinê.  A large number of potsherds, inscribed with interesting Coptic and Demotic temple records, are constantly picked up on the island by the natives, who drive a profitable trade in these valuable archives.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911); Filmer, John
Looking north from the island of Elephantinê.  At Aswân the inhabitants are still mainly of the Egyptian type, but at Elephantiné the population is wholly Nubian.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)

General view of Philae, taken from Bibbeh.  In the great temple in the centre of the view the sacred college still celebrated the mysteries of Isis and Osiris so late as A.D. 443, and thus for sixty-four years resisted the forcible conversion of Egypt to Christianity which followed the edict of Theodosius.
Manhattah, near Philae, on the Nile.  The home of many of the Shellális or boatmen of the Cataract.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)

The approach to Philae.  'In the time of the Ptolemies visitors from all parts of Egypt, travellers from distant lands, court functionaries from Alexandria, came annually in crowds to pay their vows at the tomb of the god.'
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Harley; Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
Hypaethral temple at Philae. Commonly known as 'Pharoah's bed.' One of the gems of Egypt, and exquisitely set.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Dana, William Jay (1839-1913); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924)
Nubian water-wheel.  In Nubia these sâkiyehs take the place of shadûfs of Upper Egypt, and though they are costly to erect they effect a considerable saving of labor.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Fenn, Harry (1838-1911)
The temple of Aboo Simbel, in Nubia.  The most wonderful of all the temples of Rameses the Greet, excavated in the solid rock.
Wilson, Charles William, Sir (1836-1905); Woodward, John Douglas (1846-1924); Harley
